questions.statement: Which sentence uses the subjunctive correctly after the verb 'suggest'?
questions.context: Students in Heredia are planning the school concert for June.

options.text: Marta suggested that we start the rehearsal early.
options.feedback: Correct! After 'suggested that' the clause is subjunctive, so the bare base form 'start' is required, not 'will start'.

options.text: Marta suggested that we will start the rehearsal early.
options.feedback: The modal 'will' keeps the clause indicative. A that-clause of suggestion needs the bare base form of the verb.

options.text: Marta suggested that we started the rehearsal early.
options.feedback: A past indicative form appears here. The subjunctive carries no tense, so the base form 'start' must be kept.

options.text: Marta suggested us to start the rehearsal early.
options.feedback: The pattern 'suggest someone to do' does not exist; 'suggest' takes a that-clause in the subjunctive or a gerund.

questions.explanation:
Verbs of suggestion, request and recommendation such as 'suggest', 'recommend' and 'insist' are followed by 'that' plus a subjunctive clause, which keeps the base form of the verb.

questions.statement: Which verb completes 'The doctor insisted that she ______ smoking'?
questions.context: A doctor in Heredia gives a patient a firm instruction about her health.

options.text: stops
options.feedback: A present simple form belongs to the indicative. The verb after 'insisted that' must appear as a bare base form.

options.text: will stop
options.feedback: The modal 'will' makes the clause indicative, while the subjunctive drops tense markers and negates the base form.

options.text: not smoke
options.feedback: Correct! A negative subjunctive places 'not' directly before the base form, so 'insisted that she not smoke' is right.

options.text: doesn't smoke
options.feedback: A contracted auxiliary marks tense and agreement, which the subjunctive lacks; negate the base form with 'not' instead.

questions.explanation:
The subjunctive has no tense and no agreement, so its negative is made by putting 'not' before the base form: 'insisted that he not be late', never 'that he isn't late'.

questions.statement: How should 'Carlos proposed that we should visit Monteverde' be rewritten?
questions.context: Carlos proposes a weekend trip to Monteverde for the whole class.

options.text: Carlos proposed that we will visit Monteverde.
options.feedback: Keeping a modal or replacing 'should' with 'will' leaves the clause indicative; the subjunctive needs the bare form.

options.text: Carlos proposed that we visit Monteverde.
options.feedback: Correct! 'Should' is redundant inside a that-clause after 'proposed', so the modal is dropped and 'visit' stands alone.

options.text: Carlos proposed that we visited Monteverde.
options.feedback: The past form 'visited' is indicative; a clause of proposal is not tied to a tense, so it takes the base form.

options.text: Carlos proposed us that we visit Monteverde.
options.feedback: A that-clause cannot follow an indirect object with 'us'; 'proposed' takes either a bare that-clause or a gerund.

questions.explanation:
A 'should' inside a that-clause after 'propose', 'recommend' or 'demand' is unnecessary, because the subjunctive already marks distance from reality and replaces the modal.

questions.statement: He wrote 'I suggested to her that we should cancel the trip.' What is wrong?
questions.context: A student writes about a suggestion he made to the principal of his school in Alajuela.

options.text: Nothing; the sentence is fully correct as written.
options.feedback: The sentence has two real problems, so accepting it as written would hide both a complement error and a modal error.

options.text: 'Suggested' is wrong here; the verb should be 'propose'.
options.feedback: 'Suggest' is the natural verb for a proposal, and 'propose' would still need the same subjunctive that-clause structure.

options.text: 'Cancel' is wrong, since the subjunctive needs a past form.
options.feedback: The subjunctive does not move into a past tense; it keeps the base form 'cancel' whatever the tense of the main verb.

options.text: Two problems: 'suggest' rejects 'to her', and 'should' must go.
options.feedback: Correct! 'Suggest' takes no indirect object, and the modal 'should' is redundant, so the clause must read 'that we cancel'.

questions.explanation:
Two frequent errors sit in that-clauses of suggestion: adding an indirect object after 'suggest', and leaving 'should' inside the clause. The correct text is 'suggested that we cancel the trip'.

questions.statement: Which sentence uses the subjunctive correctly with the expression 'high time'?
questions.context: The last bus from Turrialba leaves at six, so the students start to hurry.

options.text: It is high time that we left for Turrialba.
options.feedback: Correct! 'It is high time that' takes a past form as the subjunctive, and here 'left' points to the next unfulfilled moment.

options.text: It is high time that we will leave for Turrialba.
options.feedback: A future modal states a prediction, while the fixed expression 'it is high time that' demands the past subjunctive.

options.text: It is high time that we are leaving for Turrialba.
options.feedback: The present progressive describes an action in progress; the subjunctive after 'high time' always uses the simple past.

options.text: It is high time that we would leave for Turrialba.
options.feedback: 'Would' belongs to conditional and polite structures; the fixed pattern is a plain past form after 'high time that'.

questions.explanation:
Fixed expressions such as 'it is high time that', 'it is time that' and 'it is about time that' take the subjunctive in the simple past, a form borrowed from the past tense.

questions.statement: Which verb completes 'I wish I ______ more time to prepare the report'?
questions.context: Ana at a school in Cartago regrets how she spent her last term.

options.text: have
options.feedback: The bare base form points to a present reality, while a regret about the past needs the past subjunctive 'had'.

options.text: had
options.feedback: Correct! An unreal wish about the past takes the subjunctive 'had': 'I wish I had had more time to prepare it'.

options.text: will have
options.feedback: 'Will have' states a future fact, but this wish is counterfactual, so the verb of the second clause goes to the past.

options.text: am having
options.feedback: A present progressive is an indicative form; the subjunctive strips tense and keeps the single past form 'had'.

questions.explanation:
With 'wish', the verb of the second clause decides the reading: the past form 'had' signals an unreal past, as in 'I wish I had known the answer'.

questions.statement: Which verb completes 'The coach would rather that they ______ to Limon'?
questions.context: The volleyball coach in Puntarenas talks about the final his team played last weekend.

options.text: go
options.feedback: The base form fits a present or future preference, but the match happened last weekend, so the past is needed.

options.text: are going
options.feedback: The present progressive states a current situation; 'would rather' with a past reference requires the past subjunctive.

options.text: will go
options.feedback: 'Will go' points forward to a new choice, while the speaker is already looking back at last weekend.

options.text: had gone
options.feedback: Correct! 'Would rather' plus a that-clause uses the past subjunctive for a past or unreal preference: 'had gone'.

questions.explanation:
A that-clause after 'would rather' follows the subjunctive: the base form describes a present preference and the past form describes a past or unreal one, as in 'would rather that he had stayed'.

questions.statement: Which sentence uses the formal subjunctive in an 'even if' clause?
questions.context: The referee in Liberia explains that the match would go on in any weather.

options.text: Even if it were raining, the match would go on.
options.feedback: Correct! Formal concessions after 'even if' use the subjunctive 'were' because the situation is imagined, not reported.

options.text: Even if it is raining, the match will go on.
options.feedback: A present simple with 'even if' states a real possibility in the present, and 'will' turns the sentence into a prediction.

options.text: Even if it rained, the match went on.
options.feedback: The past indicative reports what actually happened, while a subjunctive condition stays unreal however it is phrased.

options.text: Even if it has rained, the match would go on.
options.feedback: The present perfect points to a real earlier rain; the subjunctive 'were raining' keeps the condition purely hypothetical.

questions.explanation:
In formal English, 'were' replaces 'was' in subjunctive conditions, including unreal concessions after 'even if', because the speaker treats the situation as imagined rather than actual.

questions.statement: Which sentence correctly complements the past form 'suggested' with a gerund?
questions.context: At a cafe in Heredia, Diego offers the group a plan for Saturday morning.

options.text: Diego suggested that going to the beach would be fun.
options.feedback: A gerund cannot stand inside a that-clause; the subjunctive there takes a bare base form, for example 'that we go'.

options.text: Diego suggested to go to the beach.
options.feedback: The bare infinitive is not an accepted complement of 'suggest'; this verb takes a gerund or a that-clause in the subjunctive.

options.text: Diego suggested going to the beach.
options.feedback: Correct! 'Suggest' accepts a gerund, 'suggested going', or a that-clause in the subjunctive, but never 'suggested to go'.

options.text: Diego suggested that we to go to the beach.
options.feedback: An infinitive cannot follow 'that'; a subjunctive that-clause needs a finite base form, so the right version is 'that we go'.

questions.explanation:
'Suggest' has two complement patterns only: a gerund, as in 'suggested going', or a that-clause in the subjunctive, as in 'suggested that we go'. The pattern 'suggested to go' is always wrong.

questions.statement: Which verb completes 'During the drill, he acted as if he ______ nothing'?
questions.context: A witness describes the strange calm of a student during the earthquake drill at a school in San Jose.

options.text: feels
options.feedback: The present simple describes a real, repeated reaction, while 'as if' here looks back at a past moment.

options.text: felt
options.feedback: Correct! 'As if' with a past reference takes the past form 'felt' as a subjunctive, presenting the calm as pretended.

options.text: has felt
options.feedback: The present perfect links the reaction to now, but the whole sequence described here is already past.

options.text: would feel
options.feedback: A conditional 'would feel' imagines a future reaction, and 'acted as if' after a past event points backwards.

questions.explanation:
The pattern 'as if' or 'as though' plus a past form is a subjunctive: it presents a comparison as imagined or pretended, which formal English prefers to a tense that claims reality.

questions.statement: Which sentence uses the subjunctive after a verb of doubt?
questions.context: A student in Alajuela reads a rumor about the new grading policy of his school.

options.text: I believe that the policy changes next year.
options.feedback: 'Believe' states an opinion the speaker accepts, so it takes the indicative rather than the subjunctive.

options.text: She supposes that every teacher agrees with the change.
options.feedback: 'Suppose' used positively means 'imagine' and keeps the indicative; its negative form would trigger the subjunctive.

options.text: I doubt that the new policy is fair to everyone.
options.feedback: Correct! 'Doubt that he is' is a classic subjunctive pattern, because the speaker keeps the claim separate from his own belief.

options.text: He thinks that the policy will surprise the students.
options.feedback: 'Thinks' reports an opinion he shares, so 'will surprise' is expected; only negated verbs of thinking use the subjunctive.

questions.explanation:
Verbs and expressions of doubt or negation trigger the subjunctive: 'doubt that', 'I don't think that', 'it is not true that'. Positive forms like 'think' keep the indicative.

questions.statement: Which verb completes 'It is essential that the equipment ______ first'?
questions.context: A lab technician in Cartago prepares the school laboratory for a safety inspection.

options.text: be
options.feedback: Correct! The passive of the subjunctive keeps 'be' unchanged, so the sentence reads 'that the equipment be checked'.

options.text: is
options.feedback: A present simple 'is' makes the clause indicative; after 'it is essential that' the passive must be 'be checked'.

options.text: will be
options.feedback: The future 'will be' predicts an event, while the subjunctive here marks necessity, not a forecast.

options.text: are
options.feedback: 'Are' is a plural agreement form that fits no subject here; the subjunctive drops agreement and keeps the bare 'be'.

questions.explanation:
The passive of the subjunctive is formed with 'be' plus a past participle, and 'be' never takes agreement: 'that the doors be locked' before the storm.

questions.statement: Rewrite it in the subjunctive: 'You should see a doctor about those headaches.' How?
questions.context: A school counselor in Santa Cruz advises a student who has headaches every week.

options.text: I recommend you see a doctor about those headaches.
options.feedback: 'Recommend' does not take an object plus a bare infinitive; it takes a that-clause or a gerund as its complement.

options.text: I recommend that you will see a doctor about those headaches.
options.feedback: The modal 'will' keeps the clause indicative, while a recommendation needs the bare base form after 'that'.

options.text: I recommend that you should see a doctor about those headaches.
options.feedback: 'Should' is redundant inside a that-clause of recommendation; the subjunctive already carries the obligatory mood.

options.text: I recommend that you see a doctor about those headaches.
options.feedback: Correct! 'Recommend that' plus the bare base form is the standard subjunctive pattern and it keeps the force of the advice.

questions.explanation:
To turn advice with 'should' into the subjunctive, place the verb after 'that' in its base form; 'should' is dropped because the subjunctive already expresses obligation.

questions.statement: Which verb completes 'If she ______ the library, her project would be ready'?
questions.context: A student in Monteverde explains why her science project was not ready last semester.

options.text: consulted
options.feedback: A bare past form reads as a real past habit, while an unreal third condition needs 'had' plus the participle.

options.text: had consulted
options.feedback: Correct! An unreal past condition uses 'had' plus the past participle, matched by the unreal result 'would have been'.

options.text: has consulted
options.feedback: The present perfect points to a consultation that really happened, but this sentence describes one that never did.

options.text: will consult
options.feedback: A future 'will consult' cannot produce a past result; 'would have been ready' already fixes the condition in the unreal past.

questions.explanation:
The if-clause of a third conditional is subjunctive: the auxiliary 'had' carries the whole unreal past, so no other tense appears and the main verb follows as a participle.

questions.statement: Which order is correct for 'recommended that every coach attend the training'?
questions.context: A school board in Alajuela debates a formal proposal about its sports program.

options.text: The board recommended every coach that attend the training in Nicoya.
options.feedback: 'Recommended' does not take an indirect object before a that-clause; the clause itself carries the subject 'every coach'.

options.text: The board recommended that every coach to attend the training in Nicoya.
options.feedback: An infinitive cannot follow 'that'; the subjunctive that-clause needs a finite base form, so 'to attend' is out.

options.text: The board recommended that every coach attend the training in Nicoya.
options.feedback: Correct! A recommendation places the subject inside the that-clause and uses the bare base form 'attend' for the subjunctive.

options.text: The board recommended that attend every coach the training in Nicoya.
options.feedback: English clauses put the verb before the subject, so this order is not grammatical even without the subjunctive issue.

questions.explanation:
Subjunctive clauses keep normal English word order: subject first, then the base form of the verb with no auxiliary, then the rest of the object, as in 'that every coach attend'.

questions.statement: Which verb completes the formal advice 'If I ______ you, I would apologize'?
questions.context: A friend in Escazu offers honest advice before a difficult conversation with a teacher.

options.text: was
options.feedback: 'Was' belongs to the indicative; formal English uses 'were' in subjunctive conditions, for every person.

options.text: am
options.feedback: 'Am' is a present simple form and fits only real conditions, but this advice imagines a situation.

options.text: be
options.feedback: 'Be' is the base form and would need a modal such as 'might'; after 'if' the subjunctive takes the past form.

options.text: were
options.feedback: Correct! 'Were' replaces 'was' in every subjunctive 'if' clause, which is why we say 'If I were you' in advice.

questions.explanation:
The subjunctive 'be' form is 'were' for every person: 'If she were here', 'If they were richer'. It marks hypothetical or imagined situations instead of facts.

questions.statement: Which is the formal way to state a purpose with the expression 'in order that'?
questions.context: A teacher in Tibas explains why she uses visual aids in her history classes.

options.text: She used posters in order that the students will remember the dates.
options.feedback: 'Will' states a definite future result, while the subjunctive 'might' expresses an aim rather than a prediction.

options.text: She used posters in order that the students might remember the dates.
options.feedback: Correct! A purpose clause after 'in order that' commonly takes the subjunctive modal 'might', which leaves the outcome open.

options.text: She used posters in order that the students remember the dates.
options.feedback: A bare present form presents the outcome as already real, but formal purpose clauses prefer 'might' here.

options.text: She used posters so that the students would remembering the dates.
options.feedback: 'Would remembering' mixes a modal with a gerund; the subjunctive needs a plain base form after 'would' or 'might'.

questions.explanation:
Formal purpose clauses introduced by 'in order that' or 'so that' often use a subjunctive modal such as 'might', because the speaker wants an outcome instead of announcing a fact.

questions.statement: Which verb completes 'Suppose that the mayor ______ the bus fare'?
questions.context: A student in Quevedo imagines how a cheaper bus fare would help the towns of her province.

options.text: will cut
options.feedback: 'Will cut' is a future indicative; 'Suppose that' introduces a hypothesis the speaker imagines, so the base form is needed.

options.text: cut
options.feedback: 'Cut' is the past form, but the subjunctive here refers to an imagined present situation, not to a past event.

options.text: cuts
options.feedback: Correct! After 'Suppose that' the subjunctive keeps the base form and its third person 's', so 'cuts' is the right choice.

options.text: is cutting
options.feedback: 'Is cutting' states a real action in progress, while the subjunctive marks a condition being invented for the argument.

questions.explanation:
Hypothetical clauses after 'suppose', 'imagine' or 'pretend' take the subjunctive, so the verb keeps the base form with third person 's' even after a past verb.

questions.statement: Which sentence breaks the subjunctive rule and needs a base form instead?
questions.context: An English teacher in San Jose marks a paragraph that four students wrote about school rules.

options.text: It is important that every student arrives on time.
options.feedback: Here the clause is indicative, because 'arrives' agrees with its subject and states a real habit; it needs 'arrive'.

options.text: The teacher insisted that we hand in the lab report.
options.feedback: Correct use of the subjunctive: 'insist' takes 'that' plus the bare base form 'hand in', with no tense marking.

options.text: She suggested that we visit the coffee farm in Turrialba.
options.feedback: Correct use of the subjunctive: 'suggest' keeps the base form 'visit', so nothing has to be corrected in this sentence.

options.text: He demanded that she be present at the hearing.
options.feedback: Correct use of the subjunctive: after 'demanded' the passive 'be present' keeps 'be' with no change in form.

questions.explanation:
A quick test is to look for tense and agreement inside the that-clause. If the verb agrees with its subject or shows a tense, it is indicative and must become the subjunctive base form.

questions.statement: Which sentence is the correct formal wording for that resolution about the library?
questions.context: A school board in Alajuela writes a formal resolution about building a new library.

options.text: The board decided that the library is built before the rainy season.
options.feedback: A present simple 'is built' is the indicative, while a board decision is a directive that needs the subjunctive passive.

options.text: The board decided that the library will be built before the rainy season.
options.feedback: 'Will be built' states a prediction rather than an official order, but a resolution expresses obligation.

options.text: The board decided that the library was built before the rainy season.
options.feedback: The past passive 'was built' reports a finished event, and the board is deciding what still has to happen.

options.text: The board decided that the library be built before the rainy season.
options.feedback: Correct! A formal decision uses the subjunctive, and in the passive the auxiliary 'be' never changes form.

questions.explanation:
Formal decisions, demands and requirements take a that-clause in the subjunctive. In the passive the auxiliary 'be' stays the same, so the clause reads 'that the library be built'.
